name: Erik Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Days I work for Hollis and Sons, a four-van firm doing rewires, fuse boards and landlord safety checks on rented houses. A landlord safety check is where you test every circuit and write a report saying the place is safe to let. Two evenings a week and some Saturdays I do my own safety checks for a handful of landlords, under my own name. I use AI every day: it drafts my reports from my test readings, writes my quotes and chases invoices.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the puzzle of a fault, and I like building something of my own on the side. What wears me out is the hours, honestly, and landlords who want a pass without fixing anything. I live with my girlfriend Nadia, she's a freelance graphic designer, and we both work from the spare room on admin nights. My plan is to go fully self-employed by next autumn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are still useful, just not magic, which is what I always thought. At Hollis I'd keep showing the others how I write reports in ten minutes. Online I'd post a short video on my setup, people like that stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I carry on with my plan. The tools I use already save me hours, and nothing in this picture takes them away. Nadia's design work stays steady too, so we're fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building the side business, aiming for 15 regular landlords by next autumn. I'd put 250 a month into a fund for a second-hand van. And I'd go self-employed on the date I planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit pleased. My plan to go self-employed works whether the AI hype is real or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest risk to going self-employed, even with nothing changing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A quiet month with a van loan. I've got about four months saved, which covers me, but only just. If two landlords sold up in the same quarter, I'd feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Mr Hollis feel about your side business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Hollis is fine with it as long as I don't take his customers, and I don't. He started the same way thirty years ago. He says the trade always needs people willing to do their own paperwork.

Save **250 a month** for a second-hand van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the best time to be in a trade, and I'd mean it. At Hollis I'd offer to set up the AI booking system. Online I'd say people should look at the trades, not just office jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my side is fine, but Nadia's isn't. Clients already ask her why they should pay for a logo when an app does one in seconds. If her work halves, we lose about a third of our household income, and my self-employment plan gets riskier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still go self-employed, maybe a few months later, once I know where Nadia's work lands. I'd use AI to run my whole office: bookings, reminders, reports, invoices, so I can do more jobs a week. And I'd help Nadia move toward work that AI can't easily do, like signage and shop fit-outs, which pairs nicely with electrics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. Not for me, for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd team up with Nadia. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shops and cafés need lighting, signs and a look. Nadia does the look, I do the wiring, and we sell it as one job. Half the cafés on our high street have terrible lighting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still go self-employed. Isn't that a risk with Nadia's income falling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. That's why I'd wait a few months and keep two months' extra savings before handing in my notice. I'd rather jump late and land well.

steps.text: Run bookings, reports and invoices through AI tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get your hands dirty, because hands-on work buys you three years. At Hollis I'd say we should all be learning to work alongside the robots. Online I'd be honest that I don't know how it ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's rough. Nadia's work is mostly gone in 2028, and my reports and quotes are done by AI too, so my side business is just testing. Then by 2031 robots can do the testing. We'd have three years where I'm the main earner and then nothing certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd drop the self-employed plan and stay at Hollis for the steady wage. I'd save every spare penny, cut the van fund, and help Nadia retrain into something hands-on, maybe sign-making or set building. And I'd learn to install and commission robots, because they'll need wiring and power.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm usually the calm one, but two earners and two exposed jobs keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd give up the self-employed plan. How does that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like losing the thing I've been building for two years. But a van loan with no certain work after 2031 would be stupid. I'd rather have a wage and a bit of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Nadia when you heard this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we'd done hard things before, like when her biggest client went bust last year. And I'd say I'll carry us for a while, and that's fine, she carried us when I was an apprentice. Then we'd make a list on the fridge.

say: I'd say **hands-on work** buys you about **three years**.
Online I'd be honest that I **don't know** how it ends.
think: Nadia's work goes in **2028**, and AI takes my **reports and quotes**.

feel: **Alarmed**, kept awake by **two exposed jobs** in one household.

fieldNote: Even an **adaptive** worker gives up his plan when both incomes are exposed.
Sees the **3-year robot gap** as breathing room, not safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ahead, if you start tomorrow. At Hollis I'd push us to become the firm that installs and services robots locally. Online I'd post what I'm learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have until 2034 before robots do the hands-on, when I'm 35. The thinking side, reports and quotes, goes in 2031, which I've mostly automated already. Nadia has five years to move, which is enough if she starts now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go self-employed on schedule but build it around robot installs and servicing, not just safety checks. I'd do a manufacturer's training course in the first year. Nadia would start a part-time course in sign-making while she still has design clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy-anxious. I'd be doing something about it every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk in betting on robot servicing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the robot makers do their own servicing, like car makers did with dealers. Then I'm a middleman nobody needs. I'd keep the safety checks going as a backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would five years change things for Nadia compared to two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Night and day. With two years my girlfriend Nadia starts from zero in a panic, and with five she can shift her clients slowly. Nadia's already better with her hands than she thinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift for anyone willing to learn. At Hollis I'd say we should plan a ten-year path, not panic. Online I'd keep posting about the tools I use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be 40 by the time robots arrive in 2039, with ten years of running my own business. That feels okay for me. Nadia's the one who'd have to change, but ten years is long enough to do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go self-employed next autumn as planned and buy the van. I'd add robot servicing to the business around year five. And Nadia and I would talk about her moving into something hands-on over the next few years, no rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the back of my mind, mostly about Nadia. For me it's mostly opportunity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change any big life plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably still get married in two years, like we said. Maybe we'd wait on buying a place until we know Nadia's next thing. I'd rather rent a bit longer than have a mortgage on one income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the trap in having ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trap in having ten years is thinking you've got ten years. The thinking AI gets good long before 2036, it's not a switch. Nadia's clients will drift away a bit every year.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it hits Nadia and me at almost the same time. What would help is cheap, fast retraining for people like her, creative people moving into hands-on work, and some kind of wage top-up while they learn. For me, clear rules on who's allowed to install and certify robots, so small firms aren't shut out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about partners. Everyone asks what happens to me, but my job's the safe one in our house.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks what happens to me, but my job's the safe one in our house.
portrait: Erik is a **27-year-old electrician** at a four-van firm with an evening **safety-check business**.
He uses **AI daily** for reports, quotes and invoices, and plans to go self-employed.
His real exposure is through his girlfriend Nadia's **design work**, which AI hits early.
Fast AGI **alarms** him enough to drop his self-employed plan for a steady wage.
With more time he builds a business around **robot installs** and helps Nadia retrain.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it hits Nadia's work and his own almost together.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap, fast **retraining** with a **wage top-up** for creative workers.
Clear rules on who can **certify robots**, so small firms aren't shut out.
